name: Oligopeptide-68

lead: Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide described in the literature as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic that inhibits the enzyme tyrosinase, which is involved in making melanin. It is sold as a skin-brightening ingredient in serums and creams.
The available human research consists of two melasma studies in which it was one component of a multi-ingredient regimen, so what it does on its own has not been separated out.

paras: According to the study authors, oligopeptide-68 inhibits tyrosinase activity, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis [1]. In one study it was paired with diacetyl boldine, which is described as stabilizing tyrosinase in its inactive form [1].

The studies reviewed here were of combination products that also contained exfoliating acids, sunscreen filters or other depigmenting agents, so adverse effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone. It is a cosmetic ingredient in the US and EU rather than a drug.

studies.title: Combined use of two formulations containing diacetyl boldine, TGF-β1 biomimetic oligopeptide-68 with other hypopigmenting/exfoliating agents and sunscreen provides effective and convenient treatment for facial melasma. Either is equal to or is better than 4% hydroquinone on normal skin.
Reflectance Confocal Microscopy Assessment of the Depigmenting Agents Complex for Melasma Treatment.
studies.source: The Journal of clinical and aesthetic dermatology

lead: Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide that is marketed as a skin-brightening ingredient. In the dermatology literature it is described as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic oligopeptide that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production [1].

Interest in looksmaxxing and skincare communities centres on its use against uneven pigmentation and melasma. The published human evidence is limited to two studies of multi-ingredient melasma regimens in which oligopeptide-68 was one component [1][2].

paras: Oligopeptide-68 appears in brightening and depigmenting cosmetic products aimed at facial hyperpigmentation such as melasma [1][2].

The authors of a 2016 melasma study describe oligopeptide-68 as inhibiting tyrosinase activity, whereas the co-formulated diacetyl boldine is described as stabilizing tyrosinase in an inactive form [1].

A 2016 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined two formulations, one containing diacetyl boldine and one containing oligopeptide-68, used together with other hypopigmenting or exfoliating agents and sunscreen for facial melasma. The study also compared them with 2% and 4% hydroquinone cream on sun-protected normal skin. The title reports that the combination provided effective and convenient treatment and that either formulation was equal to or better than 4% hydroquinone on normal skin [1].

A 2020 study used reflectance confocal microscopy to assess a depigmenting complex based on oligopeptide-68 together with phytic acid, glycolic acid, lactic acid and octinoxate in melasma, evaluating efficacy and tolerability [2]. Because both studies tested combinations, they do not isolate the effect of oligopeptide-68 itself.
